23594973_bfa534f8.text: Our current understanding of thalamocortical (TC) circuits is largely based on studies investigating so‐called ‘specific’ thalamic nuclei, which receive and transmit sensory‐triggered input to specific cortical target areas. TC neurons in these nuclei have a striking point‐to‐point topography and a stereotyped laminar pattern of termination in the cortex, which has made them ideal models to study the organization, plasticity, and development of TC circuits. However, despite their experimental importance, neurons within these nuclei only represent a fraction of all thalamic neurons and do not reflect the diversity of the TC neuron population. Here we review the distinct subtypes of projection neurons that populate the thalamus, both within and across anatomically‐defined nuclei, with regard to differences in their morphology, input/output connectivity and target specificity, as well as more recent findings on their neuron type‐specific gene expression and development. We argue that a detailed understanding of the biology of TC neurons is critical to understand the role of the thalamus in normal and pathological perception, voluntary movement, cognition and attention.
23594973_bfa534f8.section: Major neuronal classes with soma in the mouse thalamic region

23594973_ad4db142.text: Within individual nuclei such as the anterior thalamic nuclei, the mediodorsal nucleus or the pulvinar, single-cell recordings and neuroanatomical studies have started to reveal a heterogeneous population of TC neurons, with differences in the expression of calcium binding proteins, morphology, membrane properties, topographic location and target specificity

23594973_a7fbdba3.text: Certain glutamatergic neurons can also express GABAergic markers such as Slc32a1, Gad1 and Gad2 in the LGN, the mediodorsal thalamic and anterior nuclei (Perrenoud et al., 2012; Jager et al., 2016; Phillips et al., 2018). In the mediodorsal thalamic and anterior nuclei, TC neurons are positive for the excitatory neurotransmitter transporter 2 (vGluT2) and often express low levels of GABAergic markers such as Gad1 and Gad2, but very low levels of the GABA-synthetic enzymes and no GABA transporter proteins. Together, these data strongly suggest that these neurons are indeed glutamatergic and establish excitatory synapses, but may have evolved to express genes involved in GABA metabolism for other physiological purposes, perhaps to modulate the excitability or synaptic transmission properties of glutamatergic TC neurons (Jager et al., 2016; Phillips et al., 2018)
23594973_a7fbdba3.section: Developmental origin and maturation of excitatory ATN neurons

23594973_50164a40.text: .In the developing chick and mouse thalamus, there are two principal lineages of glutamatergic projection neurons that can be distinguished by the expression of Olig3 in the pTH-C and pTH-R domains or Dbx1 in the rostral-most progenitor domain (Dlx- expressing cells in the pTH-R are GABAergic interneurons). TC neurons generated from these two lineages maintain these markers in the mature thalamus, where they populate complementary groups of nuclei. Projections from Olig3-lineage nuclei terminate chiefly in middle cortical layers and generally display driver properties. In contrast, nuclei populated by Dbx1-lineage neurons project mainly to layer 1 and display modulator properties. The exact complement of thalamic nuclei generated from each lineage in rodents has not yet been described. However, fate-mapping studies in chick indicate that Olig3-lineage nuclei include sensory nuclei and probably the anterior nuclei as well, whereas the mediodorsal nucleus and intralaminar nuclei have a dual Olig3/Dbx1 origin, and the ventromedial nucleus derives from the Dbx1 lineage only (Martinez-de-la-Torre et al., 2013; Puelles et al., 2013).

23594973_c1b76e2f.text: Higher-order, matrix-like nuclei display a significantly weaker expression of PVALB and CALB than first-order nuclei (Jones and Hendry, 1989; Fortin et al., 1998; Frassoni et al., 1998). However, positive cells can be found in most nuclei, including some matrix- like nuclei such as MD or PVT (Frassoni et al., 1998).

23594973_79abbfeb.text: Thus, nuclei represent a key principle of thalamic organization and function (Sherman & Guillery, 2005;Jones, 2007). Despite the central role of nuclear parcellation in the organization of thalamocortical (TC) connectivity, there is now ample evidence for the presence of distinct TC neuron types within cytoarchitectonicallydefined nuclei (Jones, 1998)(Jones, , 2007(Rubio-Garrido et al., 2009). Such diversity mainly involves differences in the tangential spread and lamina-specific termination of TC axons in the cerebral cortex, but also in the targeting of subcortical structures such as the striatum and amygdala. At least three broad TC cell types (Herkenham, 1986)(Castro-Alamancos et al., 1997)(Jones, 1998)Jones, , 2007(Huang et al., 2000) can be identified based on such axonal differences (Table 1): intralaminar-type (IL-type), matrix-type (M-type) and coretype (C-type) neurons. Moreover, a further distinction can be made between M-type cells with widely ramified axons targeting multiple, distant cortical areas and M-type cells with an axon that arborizes within a single or few adjacent areas (Rubio-Garrido et al., 2009) (Table 1). Remarkably, these axonally-diverse neuronal subtypes are found in most thalamic nuclei, albeit in markedly varying proportions, such that a given nucleus can be defined by a typical complement of TC neuron types (Fig. 1).
